concepts.title: The Three Economic Sectors
concepts.definition: Economic activities are grouped into three sectors by what they do: the primary sector draws goods from nature, the secondary sector makes products, and the tertiary sector provides services that support both.
concepts.key_idea: Classification brings order: grouping thousands of activities into three sectors shows how the economy fits together.

concepts.title: The Primary Sector: Gifts of Nature
concepts.definition: The primary sector takes what nature offers: farming, livestock rearing, fishing, forestry and mining, the first step of every product we later buy in a shop.
concepts.key_idea: Every economy begins in the field, the forest, the sea and the mine: nature gives the first goods.

concepts.title: Secondary and Tertiary Sectors
concepts.definition: The secondary sector turns raw materials into products in factories, from pharmaceutical plants to furniture units; the tertiary sector provides services such as banking, teaching, transport, software and restaurants that support the other two.
concepts.key_idea: Making and serving: the secondary sector builds goods, the tertiary sector moves, sells and supports them.

concepts.title: How the Sectors Depend on Each Other
concepts.definition: The sectors form a chain: farms grow cotton, mills weave cloth, shops and transport sell and move it; each sector buys from and sells to the others, so growth in one lifts all.
concepts.key_idea: No sector stands alone: the shirt on your back is a relay race from field to factory to shop.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why is a teacher part of the tertiary sector while a weaver is secondary?

solution_template.explain: A weaver turns yarn into cloth, a material product; the teacher provides a service, not a thing.
Making puts the weaver in the secondary sector; serving puts the teacher in the tertiary sector.

worked_examples.question_pattern: How does cotton travel through all three sectors?

solution_template.explain: Growing cotton is primary, a gift of the soil.
Spinning and weaving make cloth, secondary; the shop that sells it and the truck that moves it are tertiary services.
